requested.title: getImage()'s original path ignores the configured maxPixels decompression-bomb guard
getImage() returns a Uint8Array aliasing the shared request-cache entry without warning callers
Browser/CDN max-age is derived from the configured TTL instead of the entry's remaining freshness, so stale and just-invalidated images get a full fresh window
cascadeSeq is a bare module-level counter in a module the build duplicates, so the unique-handler-name invariant isn't guaranteed
A failing image-cache sweep is invisible to the event bus, and sweeps can overlap
A non-finite sweepIntervalMs silently disables the image cache's only janitor

parsedVerdicts.reasoning: I confirmed the code: `imageApi.ts:127` constructs `new Bun.Image(bytes).metadata()` with no options, while `resize.ts:52` and `resize.ts:144` both thread the configured `maxPixels`. But the mitigation is structural, not incidental. Bun's own docs for `Bun.Image` state that `maxPixels` is "Checked after reading the header, **before allocating the pixel buffer**", and that `metadata()` reads "`width`, `height`, and `format` without decoding pixel data" (it "reads only the header, so it can resolve for a file that a terminal rejects"). The no-size branch never chains a transform and never awaits a terminal, so it never reaches the point the guard guards — there is no pixel buffer for a decompression bomb to inflate, and no code path downstream decodes that discarded `Bun.Image` instance. The upstream bytes are independently capped at `maxResponseBytes` (20 MB default, `fetchSource.ts:117`), and `metadata()` throwing is already caught and degraded to zero dimensions. So lowering `image.maxPixels` for untrusted sources changes nothing observable on this path: the configured limit is applied on every path that actually allocates pixels. Even under the pessimistic reading where `metadata()` did enforce `maxPixels`, the only difference would be reporting real dimensions instead of `0` for an over-limit original whose bytes are returned verbatim either way. The finding itself concedes this ("Impact is limited today… no large pixel buffer is allocated. It is the asymmetry that is the bug"), which is a defensive-consistency suggestion, not a defect — real, but with zero current behavior change and no reachable failure scenario.

The mechanics are described accurately — `getCachedOriginal` is a `requestMemo` keyed on `src` alone (L158-166), so every caller in one request awaits one promise and receives the identical `Uint8Array`, and `getImage()`'s no-size branch passes that exact reference into its public `ResolvedImage.bytes`. What refutes the finding is that this is deliberate, test-locked behavior rather than an oversight: `imageApi.requestCache.test.ts:84-87` asserts `expect(b.bytes).toBe(a.bytes)` with the comment "The shared entry is handed to every caller, bytes included." The recommended fix (`bytes: new Uint8Array(bytes)`) would break that assertion, so it is an API design change, not a bug fix. Nothing in the framework mutates the buffer: `runPipeline` hands it to `Bun.Image`, which borrows read-only (Bun's docs only warn against the *caller* mutating during a pending decode), and the debug-bar preview goes through `Buffer.from(result.bytes)`, which copies. Corruption also cannot reach disk: `FileStorage` returns binaries as lazy `BlobRef`s and `readBlobRef` materializes a fresh `Uint8Array` per read, so a mutation is confined to the current request (a same-request variant regen re-encoding from it is the only secondary effect, as the finding says, but it still requires the user to write into a buffer a framework API handed back). An implicit read-only contract on bytes returned from a cache is the near-universal convention in JS, and the authors reasoned about it explicitly in the adjacent comments (L122-123, L138-139). What remains is a legitimate documentation nit — add the caveat to `getImage()`'s JSDoc and `ResolvedImage.bytes` — not a logic bug.

The code behaves exactly as described: both success paths call `resolveImageCacheControl(options.timeToStale, options.timeToEvict, development)` (L98, L142) with the global configured window, so a response carrying `X-Mochi-Cache: stale` also carries `max-age=14400, stale-while-revalidate=72000`. But this is the documented, tested contract, unchanged since the feature landed (`git log -S` points only at #65). `packages/docs/148-images.md` states: "Served images carry an `ETag` and a `Cache-Control` derived from the cache window (`public, max-age=<timeToStale>, stale-while-revalidate=<timeToEvict − timeToStale>`)" — i.e. derived from the configured window by design — and `imageEndpoint.test.ts:11-43` locks that mapping. The same page pre-empts the finding's headline impact: "In development no `Cache-Control` is sent, so edits and `invalidateImage()` calls always show up on the next request", which is an explicit acknowledgement that in production they intentionally do not. `X-Mochi-Cache` is origin telemetry that HTTP caches ignore, so there is no protocol contradiction — an origin is entitled to assign a freshness lifetime to the representation it just served, and emitting a fixed window per response is the standard ISR-style pattern. The recommended fix is also unsound for the case it emphasizes: `MochiCache.markStale` (cache.ts:238-256) backdates only the envelope `createdAt`, while `metaFrom` derives `staleAt`/`evictAt` from the inner generation stamp `value.createdAt`, so `meta.staleAt - Date.now()` would still yield a full window right after a soft `invalidateImage()`; the endpoint would have to branch on `status` instead (the timestamps it receives cannot express a soft invalidation at all). Deriving max-age from remaining freshness would be a genuine improvement to invalidation latency, but as written this is a design critique of documented, intentional behavior, not a defect.

The code reading is correct — `cascadeSeq` is a bare module-level `let` (L130) feeding a `setHandler` name (L182), `setHandler` does replace by name (events.ts:498-509), `mochiEvents` is `pinGlobal`'d, and `requestCache.ts:178` really does pin its analogous counter for the stated reason. The analogy nonetheless fails, and that is the mitigation. `memoCounter` must be pinned because *every* bundled copy runs `requestMemo()` at module scope, so every copy mints namespaces and collisions are live. Here the counter guards a construction that is itself globally deduped: `getImageRuntime()` pins `{ options, cache }` on `globalThis.__mochi_image_runtime__` in the same module that calls `new ImageCache(...)` (config.ts:117-137), synchronously, so whichever copy — server runtime or compiled island bundle — calls it first constructs the sole instance and every other copy receives that same object. Two simultaneously live `ImageCache` instances from two different copies therefore cannot arise. `ImageCache` is not exported from `index.ts` and is unreachable through the package's `exports` map (`./image` resolves to `image/index.ts`, which exports only `Image.svelte` and types; there is no wildcard subpath), so user code cannot construct a second one either. The only multi-instance sites are tests (`imageCache.test.ts:150-154`), which run in one module copy where `++cascadeSeq` is genuinely unique. Even the exotic sequence of deleting the global and re-constructing from a different copy is benign: the earlier cache is unreferenced, so replacing its handler is the desired outcome. The finding rates itself low-confidence and "latent rather than live today"; adopting `pinGlobal` would be harmless but fixes nothing reachable.

Every specific claim checks out. `runSweep` emits `image:cache-sweep` only on the success path (L21) and funnels all failures into one `logger.warn` (L22-24) with no event; `cache:error`'s `operation` union is `'get' | 'set' | 'remove' | 'clear'` (events.ts:190), so no existing event covers a sweep failure, even though the cache subsystem does emit failure events elsewhere (`cache:error`, `cache:revalidate:failed`) — so this is a genuine hole rather than a subsystem-wide convention of silence. The load-bearing premise is confirmed: `ImageCache` builds its `FileStorage` with `purgeInterval: 0` (imageCache.ts:166), so this sweeper is the only janitor for the image cache, and for a `storage:` override like the documented `MemoryStorage({ maxAge })` too. Failure is reachable without any misconfiguration: `FileStorage.sweep` fans an uncapped `Promise.all` over every directory entry, `reportKeys: true` (which `ImageCache.sweep` always passes) adds a full `readKey` file read per expired entry, and pass 1's catch tolerates only ENOENT — so one EMFILE, EACCES, or (on Windows) an EPERM/EBUSY unlink against a concurrently-open file rejects the whole sweep, after partial progress. Repeated failures mean monotonic cache growth with `image:cache-sweep` telemetry simply going quiet. The re-entrancy gap is real too: `setInterval(runSweep, intervalMs)` with an async callback and no in-flight flag, which matters once `sweepIntervalMs` is set low or the directory is very large; overlap is not corrupting (duplicate unlinks mostly ENOENT) but duplicates FS load and can itself provoke the Windows unlink failures above. Two honest caveats that cap severity at BUG: `DEFAULT_LOG_LEVEL` is `'warn'` (utils/log.ts:23), so failures are visible on stderr by default and are only truly silent under `logLevel: 'error'`; and `FileStorage.startSweeper` has the identical log-only/no-guard shape. Both recommendations (emit a failure event, add `let running = false`) are correct and cheap.

The behavior is real — `!(intervalMs > 0)` (L13) takes the no-op branch for NaN and negatives as well as the documented `0`, and `resolveImageOptions` applies `o.sweepIntervalMs ?? 3_600_000` (config.ts:106) with no finiteness check — but the finding misstates both the trigger and the inconsistency. `undefined` never reaches the guard: the `??` default catches it, and `startImageCacheSweeper`'s parameter is typed `number`, with the only production call site passing `imageRuntime.options.sweepIntervalMs` (Mochi.ts:1721). The claimed asymmetry with "every other numeric image option" does not hold: `Number.isFinite` appears in `image/config.ts` only inside `resolveSize` (per-size width/height/quality/rotate); none of the top-level numerics — `maxPixels`, `fetchTimeoutMs`, `maxResponseBytes`, `timeToStale`, `timeToEvict` — are validated either, so `sweepIntervalMs` is unremarkable rather than an outlier, and NaN in any of those would misbehave similarly (NaN TTLs, for instance, slip past `MochiCache`'s `minTimeToStale >= maxTimeToLive` throw because NaN comparisons are false). Triggering it requires the operator to pass an out-of-contract value: the option is typed `number` and documented as "`0` disables it" in both `types.ts:141` and the docs table, and nothing in the framework or any workspace in this repo derives it from an env var. The `!(x > 0)` form is the conventional NaN-safe way to express "require a positive number", so taking the disable branch is a deliberate fail-safe against a crash or an insane interval, not a logic error. Adding a boot-time throw or warning is a reasonable, cheap hardening suggestion — but there is no defect in the code as specified, and no in-tree path reaches it.
